en: Dīgha Nikāya 26: The Discourse on the Wheel-Turning Monarch (Cakkavattisutta) 1. Being One’s Own Island and One’s Own Refuge The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there will be in the future a time when the lifespan of human beings will be eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the people will be exceedingly beautiful, possessing great radiance, and they will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, there will be a wheel-turning monarch named Saṅkha, a righteous king who rules by the Dhamma, a conqueror of the four quarters, who has attained stability in his realm, possessing the seven treasures.

He will have these seven treasures: the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh. He will have more than a thousand sons, valiant, heroic, and able to crush enemy armies. He will rule this earth, bounded by the ocean, without violence, without weapons, with righteousness, and with the law. Now, monks, at that time, the people will be exceedingly beautiful, possessing great radiance, and they will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of the wheel-turning monarch Saṅkha will give birth to a son named Vessantara. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Vessantara will give birth to a son named Sirivaḍḍha. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Sirivaḍḍha will give birth to a son named Sīhacaṇḍa. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Sīhacaṇḍa will give birth to a son named Piyaṅkara. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Piyaṅkara will give birth to a son named Mandhātā. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Mandhātā will give birth to a son named Uposatha. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Uposatha will give birth to a son named Roca. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Roca will give birth to a son named Mandiya. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Mandiya will give birth to a son named Soma. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Soma will give birth to a son named Sudassana. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Sudassana will give birth to a son named Sudatta. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Sudatta will give birth to a son named Ajita. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Ajita will give birth to a son named Vijita. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Vijita will give birth to a son named Dhammagutta. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Dhammagutta will give birth to a son named Samiddha. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years. At that time, monks, the mother of Prince Samiddha will give birth to a son named Vessabhū. He will be handsome, fair to behold, and pleasing; he will possess a golden complexion, be endowed with the marks of a Great Man, and will live for eighty thousand years."
Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was dwelling among the Magadhans at Mātulā.
There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus:
“Monks,” [the Blessed One said]. “Venerable Sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One.
The Blessed One spoke as follows:
“Monks, dwell with yourselves as an island, with yourselves as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell with himself as an island, with himself as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.”

He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… he dwells contemplating mind in mind …pe… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
"In this way, monks, a monk dwells as an island unto himself, with himself as his refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge, with no other refuge.
Monks, wander in your own range, in your ancestral domain.
Monks, as you wander in your own range, in your ancestral domain, Māra will find no opening, and Māra will find no foothold."
“Bhikkhus, it is through the undertaking of wholesome states that merit increases in this way.
2. King Daḷhanemi the Wheel-turning Monarch.

Once upon a time, bhikkhus, there was a king named Daḷhanemi, a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dhamma, conqueror of the four quarters, who had established stability in the land and was endowed with the seven treasures.”
He possessed these seven treasures, namely:
the wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Furthermore, he had more than a thousand sons who were brave, heroic in form, and capable of crushing enemy armies.
Thus, having conquered this earth bounded by the ocean without force or weapons, but by the Dhamma, he dwelt there.
Then, monks, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, King Daḷhanemi addressed a certain man:
"Good man, when you see the divine Wheel-Treasure has slipped from its place and fallen away, then report it to me."
‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ the man replied to King Daḷhanemi, monks.

Then, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, that man saw the divine Wheel-Treasure recede and fall from its place; having seen this, he went to where...
King Daḷhanemi approached him; having approached, he said this to King Daḷhanemi:
“Surely, Your Majesty, you should know that your divine wheel-treasure has slipped and fallen from its place.
Then, monks, King Daḷhanemi summoned his eldest son, the prince, and said this to him:
“Dear prince, it is said that my divine wheel-treasure has slipped from its place and fallen away.
Now I have heard this:
‘When the divine wheel-treasure of a universal monarch slips from its place and falls away, that king will not live much longer.’”
“I have indeed enjoyed human sensual pleasures; now is the time for me to seek divine sensual pleasures.
Come, dear prince, take charge of this earth bounded by the ocean.
As for me, I shall shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.”

Then, monks, King Daḷhanemi, having thoroughly instructed his eldest son, the prince, in the kingdom, shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
Seven days after that royal sage had gone forth, monks, the divine wheel-treasure disappeared.
Then, monks, a certain man approached the anointed khattiya king; having approached, he said this to the anointed khattiya king:
“‘Please know, Your Majesty, that the divine wheel-treasure has disappeared.
Then, monks, when the divine wheel-treasure had disappeared, the anointed kṣatriya king was displeased and experienced displeasure.
He approached the royal sage and, having approached him, said this to the royal sage:”
‘Please, Your Majesty, you should know that the divine wheel-treasure has disappeared.
When this was said, monks, the royal sage spoke thus to the anointed khattiya king:

‘Do not, dear son, be displeased because the divine wheel-treasure has disappeared, nor experience any state of displeasure; for the divine wheel-treasure, dear son, is not your paternal inheritance.’
Come now, dear son, conduct yourself according to the noble way of a wheel-turning monarch.
For it is possible that while you are conducting yourself in this noble way of a wheel-turning monarch, on the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight,
having bathed your head and observed the Uposatha fast, as you sit upon the upper terrace of the palace, the divine Wheel-Treasure will appear.
‘It will appear with a thousand spokes, complete with felloe and hub,
perfect in every respect. ‘But what,
sire, is that noble duty of a wheel-turning monarch?’
"In that case, my dear, relying on the Dhamma alone— honoring the Dhamma, revering the Dhamma,
esteeming the Dhamma, worshipping the Dhamma, and paying homage to the Dhamma; with the Dhamma as your banner, the Dhamma as your standard, and the Dhamma as your authority—
provide righteous protection, defense, and security for your household, your army, your kshatriyas, and your followers."
Among brahmins and householders, among those in towns and countryside, among ascetics and brahmins, and even among the beasts and birds.
And, dear son, let no practice of unrighteousness prevail in your realm.
And for those who are poor in your realm, dear son, you should provide them with wealth.
And those recluses and brahmins in your realm, dear son, who have abstained from intoxication and negligence, who are established in patience and gentleness,
who tame themselves alone, calm themselves alone, and bring themselves alone to final Nibbāna—
you should approach them from time to time, question them, and examine them thus:
“Venerable sir, what is wholesome? What is unwholesome? What is blameworthy? What is blameless? What should be cultivated?
What should not be cultivated? And what, being done by me, would lead to my harm and suffering for a long time;
or what, being done by me, would lead to my welfare and happiness for a long time?”
"Having heard them, you should avoid whatever is unwholesome and practice by undertaking whatever is wholesome.
This, dear son, is that noble conduct of a wheel-turning monarch.
2.2. The Manifestation of the Wheel-Treasure (Cakkaratana)

‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ the anointed Kṣatriya king replied to the royal seer, O monks, and he conducted himself according to the noble conduct of a wheel-turning monarch. As he was conducting himself in that noble conduct of a wheel-turning monarch,
on the fifteenth day of the Uposatha, having bathed his head and observed the Uposatha, while he had ascended to the upper terrace of his excellent palace,
the divine Wheel-Treasure appeared before him— possessing a thousand spokes, with a rim and a hub, complete in every respect.
Having seen this, it occurred to the anointed kṣatriya king:

"I have indeed heard this: 'When the divine wheel-treasure appears to an anointed kṣatriya king on the fifteenth day of the Uposatha, having bathed his head and being observant of the Uposatha while seated in the upper story of his excellent palace...'"
"It has a thousand spokes, with a rim and a hub, complete in every respect; such is the wheel-treasure of a universal monarch.
Might I indeed become a universal monarch?
Then, monks, the anointed kṣatriya king rose from his seat, arranged his upper robe over one shoulder, took the water-pitcher in his left hand, and sprinkled the wheel-treasure with his right hand:
‘May your lordship’s wheel-treasure roll forth; may your lordship’s wheel-treasure conquer!
Then, monks, that wheel-treasure rolled toward the eastern direction, and the Wheel-turning Monarch followed right behind it with his fourfold army.
And in whatever place, monks, the wheel-treasure came to a halt,
Thereupon, the Wheel-turning Monarch took up residence there together with his fourfold army.
And as for those rival kings in the eastern direction, monks, they approached the Wheel-turning Monarch and said:
“Come, Great King! Welcome to you, Great King! May you rule your own domain, Great King!”
The wheel-turning monarch spoke thus: ‘No living being is to be killed;
what is not given is not to be taken; one must not engage in sexual misconduct; one must not speak falsehood; intoxicants are not to be drunk;
and you should eat only as much as is required. And those rival kings in the eastern direction, monks, became followers of the wheel-turning monarch.
Then, monks, that Wheel-Treasure, having plunged into the eastern ocean and emerged, proceeded toward the southern direction...
[and so on] ...having plunged into the southern ocean and emerged, it proceeded toward the western direction, with the Wheel-turning King following right behind it together with his fourfold army.
And in whatever place, monks, the Wheel-Treasure came to a halt, there the Wheel-turning King took up residence together with his fourfold army.
“Now, monks, those rival kings from the western direction approached the Wheel-turning Monarch and said to him:
‘Come, great king! Welcome to you, great king! This is yours, great king; command us, great king!
The Wheel-turning Monarch replied thus:”
‘Living beings must not be killed; what is not given must not be taken; one must not engage in sexual misconduct; one must not speak falsehood; intoxicants must not be drunk;
and you should eat only as much as is required. And those rival kings in the western direction, monks, became followers of the wheel-turning monarch.

Then, monks, that Wheel-Treasure, having plunged into the western ocean and emerged again, proceeded toward the northern direction, followed by the wheel-turning monarch together with his fourfold army.
“Monks, in whatever region the Wheel-Treasure comes to rest, there the Wheel-turning Monarch takes up residence together with his fourfold army.
And those rival kings in the northern direction, monks, approach the Wheel-turning Monarch and say:
‘Come, Great King! Welcome to you, Great King! This is yours, Great King; command us, Great King!’”
The wheel-turning monarch spoke thus: ‘No living being is to be killed;
what is not given is not to be taken; one must not engage in sexual misconduct; one must not speak falsehood; intoxicants are not to be drunk;
and you should eat only as much as is required. And those rival kings in the northern direction, monks, became the followers of that wheel-turning monarch.
Then, monks, having conquered the earth as far as the ocean's edge and returned to that very royal capital,
the Wheel-Treasure stood as if fixed on its axle at the gate of the Cakkavatti king’s inner palace,
at the head of the hall of justice, beautifying the Cakkavatti king’s inner palace.
3. The Discourse on the Second and Subsequent Wheel-Turning Monarchs: "Furthermore, monks, the second wheel-turning monarch...
Furthermore, monks, the third wheel-turning monarch..."
And the fourth wheel-turning monarch, monks,
[did likewise]… and the fifth wheel-turning monarch, monks,
[did likewise]… and the sixth wheel-turning monarch, monks, [did likewise].
“Monks, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, the seventh Wheel-turning Monarch also addressed a certain man:
‘Good man, when you see the divine wheel-treasure has slipped from its place and fallen away, then report it to me.
‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ that man replied to the Wheel-turning Monarch.”
“Monks, after the passing of many years, many hundreds of years, and many thousands of years, that man saw the divine wheel-treasure recede and fall from its place.
Having seen this, he approached the Wheel-turning Monarch; having approached him, he said to the Wheel-turning Monarch:
‘Surely, Your Majesty, you should know that your divine wheel-treasure has receded and fallen from its place.’”
Then, monks, the wheel-turning monarch, having summoned his eldest son, the prince, said this to him:
“Dear prince, it seems my divine wheel-treasure has slipped from its place and fallen away. I have heard this:
when the divine wheel-treasure of a wheel-turning monarch slips and falls from its place, that monarch will not live long.”
“I have indeed enjoyed human sensual pleasures; it is now time for me to seek divine sensual pleasures. Come, dear prince, take charge of this earth bounded by the ocean.
As for me, I shall shave off my hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness.

Then, monks, the wheel-turning monarch, having thoroughly instructed his eldest son, the prince, in the kingdom, shaved off his hair and beard, donned saffron robes, and went forth from the home life into homelessness.
“Monks, seven days after the royal sage had gone forth, the divine wheel-treasure disappeared.
Then, monks, a certain man approached the anointed kṣatriya king; having approached him, he said this to the anointed kṣatriya king:
‘Sire, you should know that the divine wheel-treasure has disappeared.’”
Then, monks, when the divine wheel-treasure had disappeared, the anointed Khattiya king was displeased.
He experienced that displeasure, yet he did not approach the royal sage and ask about the noble duty of a wheel-turning monarch.
Instead, he continued to rule the country merely by means of force.
As he ruled the country with impartiality, the population did not migrate from one part to another, as was the case for former kings who practiced the noble conduct of a wheel-turning monarch.
Then, monks, the ministers, counselors, accountants, high officials, military commanders, gatekeepers, and those who lived by counsel assembled and said this to the anointed Khattiya king:

“Indeed, Your Majesty, while you have been ruling the realm with impartiality, the people do not migrate from one part of the country to another as they did under former kings who practiced the noble conduct of a wheel-turning monarch.

Yet, Your Majesty, in your kingdom there exist ministers, councilors, accountants, high officials, military commanders, gatekeepers, and those who live by counsel—both ourselves and others—who uphold the noble conduct of a wheel-turning monarch.
Pray, Your Majesty, question us regarding that noble conduct of a wheel-turning monarch.”
"Since you have asked us about that noble conduct of a wheel-turning monarch, we shall explain it to you. Then, monks,

the anointed kṣatriya king, having assembled his ministers, counselors, accountants, high officials, military commanders, gatekeepers, and those who live by counsel, questioned them regarding the noble conduct of a wheel-turning monarch.
When you asked them about the noble duty of a wheel-turning monarch, they explained it to you.
Having heard them, you indeed established righteous protection, defense, and security; however, you did not bestow wealth upon those who were destitute.
Because wealth was not bestowed upon the destitute, poverty increased to a great extent.
When poverty had reached its height, a certain man took what was not given from others, which is termed theft.
They seized him; having seized him, they brought him before the king, a kshatriya who had been anointed on the head. They said to him:
‘Your Majesty, this man has taken what was not given from others, which constitutes theft.
When this was said, monks, the anointed kṣatriya king said this to that man:
‘Is it true, my good man, that you have taken what was not given from others, which constitutes theft?’”
‘It is true, Your Majesty.
‘For what reason?
‘Because, Your Majesty, I do not live.’
Then, monks, the anointed kṣatriya king bestowed wealth upon that man, saying:
“With this wealth, my good man, support yourself; support your mother and father; support your wife and children;
engage in your work; and establish a lofty sacrificial offering for recluses and brahmins.”
‘...leading to heaven, resulting in happiness, conducive to rebirth in heaven.
‘Yes, sire,’ that man replied to the head-anointed kṣatriya king.
Then, monks, another man took what was not given from others, which constitutes theft.
They seized him.
Having seized him, they presented him to the anointed Kṣatriya king, saying:
"Your Majesty, this man has taken what was not given from others, which constitutes theft."
When this was said, monks, the anointed kṣatriya king said this to that man:
“Is it true, my good man, that you took what was not given from others, which constitutes theft?
“It is true, Your Majesty,” he replied.
‘For what reason?
‘Because, Your Majesty, I do not live.
Then, monks, the anointed kṣatriya king bestowed wealth upon that man.
“With this wealth, my good man, support yourself; support your mother and father; support your wife and children;
engage in your work; and establish a lofty sacrificial gift among ascetics and brahmins—one that leads to heaven, has a happy result, and conduces to rebirth in the celestial realms.”
‘So be it, Your Majesty,’ that man replied to the anointed Kṣatriya king, monks.
And people heard: ‘It seems, sirs, that the king bestows wealth upon those who take what has not been given by others, which is called theft.’
Having heard this, it occurred to them:
"What if we too were to take what belongs to others, in the manner of theft?
Then, monks, a certain man took what belonged to others, in the manner of theft.
They seized him.
Having seized him, they presented him to the head-anointed kshatriya king, saying:
"Your Majesty, this man has taken what was not given from others, which constitutes theft."
When this was said, monks, the anointed kṣatriya king said this to that man:
“Is it true, my good man, that you took what was not given from others, which is reckoned as theft?
“It is true, Your Majesty,” he replied.
‘For what reason?
‘Because I do not live, Your Majesty.
Then, monks, it occurred to that anointed Kṣatriya king:
‘If I were to provide wealth for whoever among others takes what is not given, which is called theft, then this taking of what is not given will increase.
What if I were to suppress this man thoroughly, crush him to the roots, and cut off his head?
Then, monks, the anointed kṣatriya king gave orders to his men:
“In that case, my good man, bind this man’s arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope,
shave his head, and lead him around from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads to the accompaniment of a harsh-sounding drum.
Then, having exited through the southern gate, suppress him thoroughly to the south of the city.”
“‘Execute him by the roots! Cut off his head!
‘Yes, Your Majesty,’ those men replied to the anointed Khattiya king, and having bound that man’s arms tightly behind his back with a strong rope and shaved his head, they led him away.”
Leading him from street to street and from crossroads to crossroads with the loud-sounding drum,
they went out through the southern gate and executed a thorough suppression to the south of the city;
they hacked him down by the roots and cut off his head.
“Bhikkhus, people heard:
‘It seems, sirs, that King Sunisedha punishes those who take what is not given from others by way of theft; he eradicates them root and branch and cuts off their heads.
Having heard this, it occurred to them:”
‘What if we were to have sharp weapons made? Having had sharp weapons made, we shall utterly suppress those from whom we take what is not given by way of theft;
we shall strike them down at the root and cut off their heads.’

They had sharp swords made; having had sharp swords made, they set about destroying villages, they set about destroying market towns, they set about destroying cities, and they set about plundering highways.
Those from whom they took what was not given, considering it theft, they utterly suppressed, they exterminated by the roots, and they cut off their heads.
Thus, monks, when wealth was not bestowed upon the poor, poverty increased;
when poverty had increased, taking what was not given increased; when taking what was not given had increased, weapons increased;
when weapons had increased, the taking of life increased; when the taking of life had increased—
As those beings passed away, their lifespan decreased and their beauty also decreased.
While their lifespan and beauty were thus diminishing, among humans whose lifespan was eighty thousand years, there arose sons whose lifespan was forty thousand years.
Among those humans, O monks, whose lifespan was forty thousand years, a certain man took what was not given, which is called theft.
They seized him.
Having seized him, they presented him to the head-anointed kṣatriya king, saying:
“Sire, this man has taken what was not given from others, which constitutes theft.”
When this was said, monks, the anointed kṣatriya king said this to that man:
“Is it true, my good man, that you took what was not given from others, in the manner of theft?
“No, Your Majesty,” he replied, speaking a deliberate lie.
Thus, monks, when wealth was not bestowed upon the poor, poverty increased.
When poverty had increased, taking what was not given increased. When taking what was not given had increased, weapons increased.
When weapons had increased, the killing of living beings increased. When the killing of living beings had increased—
When false speech had increased, the lifespan of those beings diminished and their beauty also diminished.
As their lifespan and beauty were diminishing, the sons of humans who had a lifespan of forty thousand years came to have a lifespan of twenty thousand years.
Among those humans with a lifespan of twenty thousand years, O monks, a certain man took what was not given, which is called theft.
Then a certain man informed a head-anointed kṣatriya king:
“Sire, a man named so-and-so has taken what was not given from others by way of theft.
Thus he slandered him. In this way, monks, when wealth was not bestowed upon the poor, poverty reached its full extent.
When poverty reached its peak, the taking of what was not given reached its peak; when the taking of what was not given reached its peak, the sword reached its peak;
when the sword reached its peak, the killing of living beings reached its peak;
when the killing of living beings reached its peak, false speech reached its peak; when false speech reached its peak, malicious speech reached its peak.
When malicious speech had become widespread, the lifespan of those beings diminished and their beauty also diminished.
As their lifespan and their beauty were diminishing, among humans whose lifespan was twenty thousand years, there were children whose lifespan was ten thousand years.
Among humans with a ten-thousand-year lifespan, monks, some beings were beautiful, while other beings were ugly.
Therein, those beings who were ugly, coveting those beings who were beautiful, engaged in sexual misconduct with the wives of others.
Thus, monks, when wealth was not bestowed upon the poor, poverty increased.
When poverty had increased... [as before] ...sexual misconduct increased; when sexual misconduct had increased...
As those beings passed away, their lifespan diminished and their beauty also diminished.
While their lifespan and beauty were thus diminishing, among humans whose lifespan was ten thousand years, there arose children whose lifespan was five thousand years.
Among those humans, monks, whose lifespan was five thousand years, two things reached a state of abundance:
Harsh speech and idle chatter.
When these two qualities became widespread, the lifespan of those beings declined and their beauty also declined.

As their lifespan and beauty were declining, among humans whose lifespan was five thousand years, some had sons with a lifespan of two thousand five hundred years, and some had sons with a lifespan of two thousand years.
“Bhikkhus, when the lifespan of human beings was two thousand five hundred years, covetousness and ill will reached a state of abundance.
When covetousness and ill will had reached abundance, the lifespan of those beings declined, and their beauty also declined.
As their lifespan and their beauty were declining, the children of those human beings who had a lifespan of two thousand five hundred years came to have a lifespan of one thousand years.”
“Bhikkhus, among humans with a life span of a thousand years, wrong view became prevalent.
When wrong view had become prevalent, the life span of those beings declined, and their beauty also declined.
As their life span was declining and their beauty was declining, the children of those humans with a life span of a thousand years came to have a life span of five hundred years.”
“Monks, among human beings with a lifespan of five hundred years, three things reached their peak:
lust for what is contrary to the Dhamma, unjust greed, and wrong Dhamma.
When these three things had reached their peak, the lifespan of those beings declined, and their beauty also declined.”

As their lifespan was declining and their beauty was declining, among humans whose lifespan was five hundred years, some had sons with a lifespan of two hundred and fifty years, and some had sons with a lifespan of two hundred years.
Monks, when humans had a lifespan of two hundred and fifty years, these things came to abundance:
lack of respect for mother, lack of respect for father, lack of respect for recluses, lack of respect for brahmins, and lack of deference toward elders in the family.
Thus, monks, when wealth was not bestowed upon those who were destitute, poverty increased.
When poverty had increased, the taking of what was not given increased.
When the taking of what was not given had increased, the sword increased.
When the sword had increased, the taking of life increased.
When the taking of life had increased, false speech increased.
When false speech had increased, malicious speech increased.
When divisive speech had increased, sexual misconduct reached a state of increase.
When sexual misconduct had increased, two things reached a state of increase: harsh speech and idle chatter.
When these two things had increased, covetousness and ill will reached a state of increase.
When covetousness and ill will had increased, wrong view increased.
When wrong view had increased, three things increased: delight in what is contrary to the Dhamma, immoderate greed, and adherence to false doctrines.

When these three things had increased, these things increased: lack of respect for mothers, lack of respect for fathers, lack of respect for ascetics, lack of respect for brahmins, and lack of reverence for those who are senior in their own family.
When these things had reached such abundance, the lifespan of those beings diminished, and their beauty also diminished.
As their lifespan was diminishing and their beauty was diminishing, among humans whose lifespan was two hundred and fifty years, there were sons with a lifespan of one hundred years.
5. The Period of the Ten-Year Lifespan.
"There will come a time, monks, when the children of these humans will have a lifespan of ten years.
When humans have a ten-year lifespan, monks, girls of five years will be marriageable.
When humans have a ten-year lifespan, monks, these flavors will disappear, namely: [the list of flavors follows]."
Ghee, fresh butter, oil, honey, molasses, and salt.
Monks, among humans with a lifespan of ten years, kudrūsaka will be the foremost of foods.
Just as, monks, at present rice and meat are the foremost of foods.
In the same way, monks, among humans with a lifespan of ten years, kudrūsaka will be the foremost of foods.
Among humans with a lifespan of ten years, monks, the ten courses of wholesome action will completely disappear, and the ten courses of unwholesome action will flourish excessively.
Among humans with a lifespan of ten years, monks, even the word "wholesome" will not exist; how much less, then, a doer of what is wholesome?

“Bhikkhus, among those humans with a lifespan of ten years, those who will be disrespectful toward their mothers, disrespectful toward their fathers, disrespectful toward recluses, disrespectful toward brahmins, and who do not honor their elders in the family, they will be the ones who are honored and praised.

Just as, bhikkhus, at present those who are respectful toward their mothers, respectful toward their fathers, respectful toward recluses, respectful toward brahmins, and who honor their elders in the family are honored and praised; so it will be then.”

In the same way, monks, among those humans with a lifespan of ten years, those who are disrespectful toward their mothers, disrespectful toward their fathers, lacking in the conduct of a recluse, lacking in the conduct of a brahmin, and not honoring their elders in the family, will be the ones who are honored and praised.

Monks, among those humans with a lifespan of ten years, there will be no such thing as "mother," or "maternal aunt," or "maternal uncle’s wife," or "the wife of a teacher," or "the wife of one's elders.
The world will fall into a state of promiscuity, just like goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, dogs and jackals.
“Bhikkhus, when the lifespan of human beings is ten years, those beings will harbor intense malice toward one another, intense ill will, intense mental corruption, and intense murderous intent.
Mothers will feel it toward their sons, and sons toward their mothers;
fathers will feel it toward their sons, and sons toward their fathers.”

A brother will have a fierce resentment toward his sister, and a sister will have a fierce resentment toward her brother; there will be fierce ill will, fierce malice of mind, and a fierce intent to kill.
Just as, monks, when a hunter sees a deer, a fierce resentment arises, a fierce ill will, a fierce malice of mind, and a fierce intent to kill.

In the same way, monks, when human beings have a lifespan of ten years, those beings will harbor toward one another intense resentment, intense ill will, intense malice of mind, and intense murderous intent.
Even a mother toward her son, and a son toward his mother;
even a father toward his son, and a son toward his father.

A brother will harbor intense resentment toward his sister, and a sister will harbor intense resentment toward her brother; there will be intense ill-will, intense malice of mind, and an intense murderous intent.
Monks, among humans with a lifespan of ten years, there will be an intermediate eon of weapons for seven days.
They will perceive one another as wild beasts.
Sharp swords will appear in their hands.
With those sharp swords, they will deprive one another of life, saying, "This is game!
This is game! Then, bhikkhus, it will occur to some of those beings:

‘Let us not harm anyone, nor let anyone harm us; what if we were to enter a thicket of grass, a thicket of forest, a thicket of trees, a river gorge, or a mountain cleft, and subsist there on roots and fruits from the forest?
They will enter a thicket of grass, a thicket of forest, a thicket of trees, a river gorge, or a mountain cleft, and for seven days they will subsist on roots and fruits from the forest.

At the end of those seven days, those beings will emerge from the thickets of grass, the thickets of forest, the thickets of trees, the river ravines, and the mountain crags; they will embrace one another and console one another, saying:
“O beings, you have been seen! You live! O beings, you have been seen! You live! 6.
Discourse on the Increase of Life Span, Beauty, and Other Qualities.
Then, monks, it will occur to those beings:
"It is indeed because of our undertaking of unwholesome states that we have come to such a long-lasting destruction of our kin.
What if we were now to do what is wholesome?"
"What wholesome deed might we do?
Suppose we were to abstain from taking life; having undertaken this wholesome practice, let us abide by it.
They will abstain from taking life; having undertaken this wholesome practice, they will abide by it.
“Because of their undertaking of wholesome states, they will increase in lifespan and increase in beauty.
As their lifespan and beauty increase, the children of those humans who have a ten-year lifespan will have a twenty-year lifespan.
Then, monks, it will occur to those beings:”
‘It is indeed because of our undertaking of wholesome qualities that we increase in lifespan and increase in beauty.
What if we were to perform even more wholesome deeds?
What wholesome deed might we perform?’
"Perhaps we should abstain from taking what is not given...
abstain from sexual misconduct...
abstain from false speech..."
We shall abstain from malicious speech;
we shall abstain from harsh speech;
we shall abstain from idle chatter.
We should abandon covetousness… we should abandon ill will… we should abandon wrong view…
‘We should abandon three things:

unrighteous greed, improper covetousness, and wrong doctrine… What if we were to be filial toward our mothers, filial toward our fathers, respectful toward recluses and brahmins, and honoring those who are senior in our families; having undertaken this wholesome practice, let us live accordingly.’”

They will be filial toward their mothers, filial toward their fathers, respectful toward recluses and brahmins, and honoring those who are elders in their families; they will live having undertaken this wholesome Dhamma.
Because of their undertaking of wholesome states, they will increase in lifespan and increase in beauty.
As their lifespan and beauty increase, among humans whose lifespan is twenty years, there will be sons with a lifespan of forty years. …
Of humans with a forty-year lifespan, there will be children with an eighty-year lifespan;
of humans with an eighty-year lifespan, there will be children with a six-hundred-year lifespan;
of humans with a six-hundred-year lifespan, there will be children with a two-thousand-year lifespan.
The sons of those humans with a lifespan of one hundred and twenty years will have a lifespan of six hundred and forty years.
The sons of those humans with a lifespan of six hundred and forty years will have a lifespan of two thousand years.
… The sons of those humans with a lifespan of two thousand years will have a lifespan of four thousand years. …
The children of humans with a life span of four thousand years will have a life span of eight thousand years;
the children of humans with a life span of eight thousand years will have a life span of twenty thousand years;
the children of humans with a life span of twenty thousand years will have a life span of forty thousand years.
The sons of humans with a lifespan of forty thousand years will have a lifespan of eighty thousand years...
among humans with a lifespan of eighty thousand years, monks, girls who are five hundred years old will be marriageable.
7. The Arising of King Saṅkha.
“Monks, among humans with a lifespan of eighty thousand years, there will be three afflictions: desire, hunger, and old age.
Monks, among humans with a lifespan of eighty thousand years, this Jambudīpa will be prosperous and flourishing, with villages, towns, and royal capitals as close together as a cock’s flight.
Monks, among humans with a lifespan of eighty thousand years, this Jambudīpa will be as if packed with people, like a thicket of reeds or a thicket of rushes.”

“Monks, when human beings have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, this Bārāṇasī will become a royal capital named Ketumatī—prosperous, flourishing, populous, crowded with people, and well-supplied with food.
Monks, when human beings have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, there will be eighty-four thousand cities in this Jambudīpa, with the royal capital Ketumatī as their chief.
Monks, when human beings have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, in the royal capital of Ketumatī, there will be one named Saṅkha...”
A king shall arise, a wheel-turning monarch, righteous, a king of Dhamma, conqueror of the four quarters,
who has attained stability in his realm and is endowed with the seven treasures. These are his seven treasures, namely:
The wheel-treasure, the elephant-treasure, the horse-treasure, the jewel-treasure, the woman-treasure, the householder-treasure, and the counselor-treasure as the seventh.
Moreover, he will have more than a thousand sons, valiant, of heroic form, and crushers of enemy armies.
Having conquered this earth, bounded by the ocean, without punishment and without weapon, through righteousness alone, he will dwell as its ruler.

8. The Arising of the Buddha Metteyya: "Monks, when human beings have a lifespan of eighty thousand years, a Blessed One named Metteyya will arise in the world—an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, perfect in knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed."
The Teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.

Just as I have now arisen in the world as an Arahant, a perfectly enlightened Buddha, endowed with knowledge and conduct, a Sugata, a knower of the worlds, an unsurpassed charioteer of men to be tamed, a teacher of gods and humans, a Buddha, a Blessed One;
he [the Tathāgata] [understood] this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its gods and humans...

Having realized it for himself through direct knowledge, he will proclaim it—just as I, at present, having realized this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, this generation with its ascetics and brahmins, its princes and people, have realized it for myself through direct knowledge and proclaim it.

He will teach the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing; he will reveal the holy life in its entirety, perfectly complete and pure.
"Just as I now teach the Dhamma— good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end, with the right meaning and phrasing, proclaiming the holy life in its entirety, perfectly pure—
even so will he lead a community of many thousands of bhikkhus, just as I now lead a community of many hundreds of bhikkhus. Then, monks,
King Saṅkha will take that sacrificial post which was caused to be made by King Mahāpanāda."
Having raised that sacrificial post, having dwelt there, having given it away and released it, and having bestowed gifts upon ascetics, brahmins, the poor, the destitute, the wayfarers, and beggars,
he will shave off his hair and beard, don saffron robes, and go forth from the home life into homelessness in the presence of the Blessed One Metteyya, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
Having thus gone forth, dwelling alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute, before long he will,

by realizing it for himself with direct knowledge, here and now enter upon and abide in that supreme goal of the holy life, for the sake of which clansmen rightly go forth from the home life into homelessness.
“Monks, dwell with yourselves as an island, with yourselves as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge.
And how, monks, does a monk dwell with himself as an island, with himself as a refuge, with no other refuge; with the Dhamma as an island, with the Dhamma as a refuge, with no other refuge?
Here, monks, a monk dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.”

He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings …pe… he dwells contemplating mind in mind …pe… he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
In this way, monks, a monk dwells as an island unto himself, with himself as his refuge and no other refuge; with the Dhamma as his island, with the Dhamma as his refuge and no other refuge.
9. Discourse on Increasing Longevity, Beauty, and Other Qualities of a Monk "Monks, move within your own range, in the domain of your ancestors."

“Bhikkhus, while walking in their proper range, within their own ancestral domain, you will increase in lifespan, you will increase in beauty, you will increase in happiness, you will increase in wealth, and you will increase in strength.
And what, bhikkhus, is a bhikkhu’s lifespan?
Here, bhikkhus, a bhikkhu develops the basis for psychic power that possesses concentration due to desire and volitional formations of striving.”
He develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of energy and volitional formations of striving;
he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of mind and volitional formations of striving;
he develops the basis for psychic power endowed with concentration of investigation and volitional formations of striving.
Thus, by having developed and cultivated these four bases of psychic power, he could, if he so desired, remain for an eon or for the remainder of an eon.
This, monks, is the monk’s excellence in regard to life.
And what, monks, is the monk’s excellence in regard to beauty?

"Here, monks, a monk is virtuous; he dwells restrained by the Pātimokkha, possessed of proper conduct and resort, seeing danger in even the slightest faults, and having undertaken them, he trains himself in the rules of training.
This, monks, is the beauty of a monk.
And what, monks, is the happiness of a monk?"

Here, monks, a monk, secluded from sensual pleasures and secluded from unwholesome states, enters and dwells in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by applied thought and sustained thought, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion.
With the stilling of applied and sustained thought... [he enters] the second jhāna...
the third jhāna...
He enters and dwells in the fourth jhāna.
This, monks, is what constitutes a monk’s happiness.
And what, monks, is a monk’s wealth?
Here, monks, a bhikkhu dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with loving-kindness,
likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth. Thus above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself,
he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness— vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity.
He dwells pervading with a mind imbued with non-affliction.
With a mind imbued with compassion …pe… with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy …pe…
He dwells pervading one quarter with a mind imbued with equanimity. Likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth.
Thus above, below, across, everywhere, in every way, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, immeasurable, free from enmity, and free from ill will.
This, monks, is the monk’s wealth.
And what, monks, is the monk’s strength?

Here, monks, with the destruction of the taints, a monk dwells having realized for himself with direct knowledge, in this very life, the taintless liberation of mind and liberation by wisdom, and having entered upon it.
“This, monks, is the power of a monk.
Monks, I do not see even a single other power that is so difficult to overcome as this power of Māra.
It is, monks, because of the undertaking of wholesome states that merit increases in this way.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Delighted, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The third discourse, the Cakkavatti Sutta, is finished.
